BL-287.design:
MEASURED, NOT SUSPECTED (2026-08-04). A full verify-tier rebuild was taking 45-90 minutes and
blocking a session. The cause is one line: CMakeLists.txt:433

    add_executable(${harness_name} "${harness_src}" ${IO_WORLD_SOURCES})

Every harness target compiles the ENTIRE world layer from source. With 44 harnesses in
tools/verify/ and 30 world TUs in IO_WORLD_SOURCES, that is 1,320 compilations of the same 30
files per clean build. The object files are byte-identical across all 44 targets; only the
harness TU differs.

THE FIX. Compile the world layer once as an OBJECT library and link every harness against it:

    add_library(io_world_obj OBJECT ${IO_WORLD_SOURCES})
    target_include_directories(io_world_obj PUBLIC src)
    # per harness:
    add_executable(${harness_name} "${harness_src}" $<TARGET_OBJECTS:io_world_obj>)

That takes the world-layer compilation count from 1,320 to 30 — a 44x reduction on the
dominant cost. Harness TUs (44) stay as they are. Nothing about the harnesses themselves
changes; this is purely how the same objects are produced.

SECOND, SMALLER WIN. target_precompile_headers is applied only to ProjectIo (CMakeLists.txt:153),
so the harness tier — which is the overwhelming majority of the compiling — gets no PCH benefit.
The OBJECT library is the natural place to attach one.

ADJACENT, NOT PART OF THIS ITEM. The default build/ directory is configured NMake Makefiles +
Debug, which is single-threaded (15 of 16 cores idle) and produces harnesses that run ~30x
slower than Release. A build_rel/ directory already exists configured Ninja + Release and is
simply not the default anyone reaches for. Worth a line in DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES pointing at
it; that is documentation, not this code change.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING. This is not a micro-optimisation: it is the difference between a
verify-tier rebuild being a coffee break and being a session-ending event. Any change to a
widely-included header (components.hpp, world.hpp) currently invalidates all 1,320. The
BL-286 resource_type extension did exactly that and cost this session most of an hour.

VERIFICATION. Time a clean build of the verify tier before and after, and confirm ctest still
passes the same set. The object-library form must produce identical binaries — if any harness
behaves differently, something was depending on per-target compile flags and that is the real
finding.

BL-288.design:
FOUND BY SWITCHING BUILD DIRECTORIES (2026-08-04), not by a code change. A full ctest run in
build_rel/ (Ninja + Release) reports 4 of 44 failing: ai_skill_harness, data_creep_harness,
settlement_harness, world_audit.

THEY ARE PRE-EXISTING, and that is established rather than assumed. BL-286 extended
resource_type and five ctest failures appeared, so the three BL-286 source files were reverted
to the pre-merge commit and the failing targets rebuilt and re-run. Result: prospective_profit
PASSED pre-merge (that one was a real BL-286 regression, fixed by value-initialising the
resource arrays in components.hpp). These four FAILED pre-merge too. They are not caused by

THE ACTUAL PROBLEM IS THAT NOBODY KNEW. The default build/ directory is configured NMake +
Debug, and that is what every session reaches for. build_rel/ (Ninja + Release) exists and is
not the default. So the Release tier can fail indefinitely without surfacing. At least

build.

WHY CONFIGURATION-DEPENDENT FAILURES DESERVE PRIORITY. Debug fills fresh allocations with a
pattern; Release does not. A test that passes only in Debug is usually reading uninitialised
memory or relying on some other undefined behaviour that the optimiser is entitled to change.
The BL-286 NaN was exactly this shape — market_component::price and three siblings had no
initialiser and had been relying on every slot being authored — and it had been latent in the
code waiting for anyone to extend the enum. Four more Release-only failures plausibly hide
more of the same.

symptom so far: settlement_harness fails "S7d the world-level diversity floor holds across the
corporation set". The others were not diagnosed. Then decide the standing rule — either the
Release tier is green and stays green, or the project states plainly that Debug is the
supported configuration and Release is unsupported. The current position, where Release is
available, faster, and quietly broken, is the worst of the three.

BL-288.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.8). THE PREMISE WAS HALF RIGHT AND THE MEASUREMENT CHANGED THE FIX. The item said four harnesses fail in Release and nobody noticed because the default tree is Debug. On Linux the canonical tree (build_linux) is now Ninja + RELEASE, so the Debug/Release blindness is already gone here — and a full Release run reported TEN failures, of which exactly ONE was a failing assertion. Each was run alone on an idle machine to find out which: earthlike_lean_trace 121s PASSES, notable_worlds 105s PASSES, mediterranean_sweep 87s PASSES, earthlike_tile_census 58s PASSES (2s under the bound, i.e. passing by luck) — four reported as Timeout purely because every harness carried a flat 60s bound. history_sim_harness and history_sweep did not finish in 400s. econ_stability and home_surface_bench both PASS standalone and failed only because a concurrent build was loading the machine — they assert ABSOLUTE wall-clock times. world_audit fails 1 of 26 assertions, a world-generation finding (BL-291). ai_skill_harness was the single real defect: stale GCC goldens, fixed under BL-285. FIX: three tiers in CMakeLists.txt. Default 60s; IO_TEST_TIMEOUT_LONG raised 120s -> 240s and widened to cover the four measured slow-but-bounded harnesses; a `sweep` label with NO timeout for history_sim_harness/history_sweep, which are open-ended research tools rather than gate tests and are excluded from the routine gate; and a `bench` label on the two wall-clock assertions so a failure there reads as 're-run it idle' rather than as a regression. The documented gate becomes `ctest --test-dir build_linux -LE sweep --output-on-failure` (53 tests). DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md § Merge gate gains the tier table and the reason: a red suite that is mostly noise trains you to ignore it, which is precisely how the one real defect sat unnoticed among nine false positives.

BL-290.design:
FOUND BY THE DOCUMENTATION AUDIT (2026-08-04), reading code against the standing rule added
2026-08-03: "Real history is a mechanism reference, never a name source." The docs passed that
sweep clean. The code did not.

TWO SITES.

1. nation_generation.cpp:577-608 — Pass 5 naming. Two problems, and the second is the worse one.
   (a) The bank is recognisably Latin/European: codas "ia", "us", "is", "or"; onset "Lun"; nouns
   "Republic", "Commonwealth", "Principality", "Protectorate"; adjectives "Free", "United",
   "Sacred". That is trap #1 named in GENERATION_STRATEGY.md's own transfers/does-not table —
   "culture-flavoured" must not mean "Earth-culture-flavoured".
   (b) The bank is GLOBAL. It does not read the per-culture phonology that creeds.cpp:64-82
   already rolls, so a nation's gods and the nation's own name come from unrelated sound systems.
   NATION_GENERATION.md § Pass 5 claims the bank is "culture-flavoured"; it is not culture-derived
   at all.

2. city_names.cpp:8-22 — synthetic, but the morphemes are English: "ton", "ford", "haven",
   "burg". Same trap, milder, same fix class.

WHY (b) IS THE INTERESTING HALF. The fix is not "pick less Roman-sounding syllables" — that just
moves the accent. The generator already produces a per-culture phonology upstream; naming should
CONSUME it, so a culture's names, gods and places share one sound system as a consequence of the
chain rather than by coincidence. That is the house pattern (generation as consequence, not dice)
and it makes the Earth-flavour problem structurally impossible rather than merely corrected.

NOT IN SCOPE: body names (Helios, Kepler, Selene, Pallas, Cinder) are Greek/Latin astronomy words,
pre-existing and deliberate — Ben's call if that ever changes.

RELATED: BL-257 (generated body names) is the sibling item on the body axis.
BL-290.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.10). The fix is CONSUMPTION, exactly as the item argued: naming now reads the per-culture phonology the generator already produces, rather than picking less-Roman syllables from a global bank. NEW `src/world/tongue.{hpp,cpp}` lifts the phoneme inventory, the word builder and `coin_lexicon` out of creeds.cpp so downstream passes can consume them; templated on the RNG with an `mt_picker` adapter, so the creeds' splitmix stream and the generation passes' mt19937 share one word-builder. creeds.cpp's own roll is byte-for-byte unchanged (same pick() calls, same order) -- it now RETAINS the tongue on `culture::speech` instead of discarding it. SITE 1 (nation_generation.cpp): the whole Latin/European bank -- k_onsets/k_nuclei/k_codas/k_adjectives/k_nouns -- is DELETED. hard_coded_world.cpp carries each province's tongue into a new `nation_params::seed_tongues`, parallel to the existing seed_tiles anchors; Pass 5 gives each nation the speech of the lowest-indexed seed still inside it after the merge pass and names it in that tongue. SITE 2 (city_names.cpp): the English morpheme bank (ton/ford/haven/burg) is gone. Population centres are placed BEFORE creeds exist, so they are first named from a body-level tongue then re-named by a new `name_population_centres` using the NEAREST province's culture -- the same 'whose gods' rule settlement already uses. NOUNS AND ADJECTIVES WERE GENERATED, NOT DROPPED. Each tongue coins its own words for realm/town/epithet via `coin_lexicon`, which is a PURE FUNCTION OF THE TONGUE -- its stream is seeded by hashing the inventory, not by any caller's RNG. That is what lets nation naming and city naming coin identical morphemes for a culture without sharing a stream or passing words between passes. Dropping the scaffolding would have cost the political map its variety of name SHAPE; this keeps the shape and makes a shared morpheme a visible marker of kinship. SAMPLE (default seed) -- nations: Kemua, Kuamreiteik Tekua, Lu Lakaka, Luthai Muda, Luthai Saikra, Mathkhei Khedath, Ramhihom Zamto, Rerekua Tekua, Ruaruath, Sheldede Shuashua, Tair Memek, Tuavaivuath Vuari, Vuaththi Vuari, Zorzelzo Vuthe. Cities: Damuthrai, Duagual, Hilshesre, Kereimtem, Khualmes, Mitaikri, Shualgual, Thaithairi, Thi Ruari, Tholre Shergual, Vegual, Vushor. THE KINSHIP IS EMERGENT, NOT AUTHORED: Rerekua Tekua / Kuamreiteik Tekua share a realm word; Tuavaivuath Vuari / Vuaththi Vuari likewise; Duagual / Shualgual / Vegual share a settlement morpheme; Luthai Muda / Luthai Saikra share an epithet. That is the house pattern working -- generation as consequence rather than dictionary lookup. DETERMINISM: world_determinism ALL PASS, determinism_harness OK, plus creeds_harness (13), settlement_harness (21), history_ladder_harness and era_world_harness (12). The sample printer was run in two separate processes and diffed identical. All new randomness goes through existing seeded streams or the data-derived tongue hash. TWO DELIBERATE NON-FIXES, both recorded rather than hidden. (1) creeds.cpp's DOMAINS and EPITHETS ('the sea', 'who counts the spears') stay English BY DESIGN -- the header states the common-trade-tongue rule, so prose goes common while proper names stay native. BL-513.design:
## Ben's ruling (2026-08-21, design form)

> "We can use a heuristic of area, infrastructure, habitability and population.
> I.e. how much can this land sustain. Whereas per-tile limits are based on the
> richness of the underlying deposit. Building limits do not determine between
> different types of building. So it does not matter if you can build 60
> buildings, whether they are 5 of one type and 5 of another, or 10 of one type."

## Two limits, two different questions

They coexist; neither replaces the other.

| Limit | Grain | Asks | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extraction stack cap (exists) | tile | may this deposit support another site? | deposit richness |
| **Building limit (this item)** | **province** | **how much can this land sustain?** | **area + infrastructure + habitability + population** |

The province limit is **type-agnostic** by ruling: it bounds the TOTAL, and the
mix inside it is the player's business. That is what makes it a statement about
land rather than a balance dial on building types.

## What the heuristic must not become

A picked number. BL-463 pinned the settlement divisor by measurement and this
follows it: derive the shape from the four inputs, then pin any coefficient
against `province_capacity_probe`'s spread across seeds, and report the spread in
the item. `substrate_census` and the probe are the instruments.

The four inputs, in the order Ben named them:
- **Area** — land tiles in the province (ocean excluded, as the probe already counts).
- **Infrastructure** — roads/hubs. Note this makes the limit MOVE during play, which
  neither existing cap does: building a road would raise a ceiling. That is a real
  and desirable coupling (BL-325's ruling 3 makes reach one field) but it is also
  the first ceiling in the game that is not fixed at generation. Worth confirming
  it is intended to be dynamic rather than read once.
- **Habitability** — already on the tile (TILES.md / POPULATION.md).
- **Population** — population centres in or near the province.

## Honest note on what this will and will not do today

It will NOT increase what generation builds. `province_capacity_probe` measured
the world at **0.13% of existing capacity used**, zero tiles at their cap, and
the fullest province holding 3 buildings against a capacity of 16. Nothing is
being refused, so a new ceiling refuses nothing either.

Its value is forward: it is the ceiling that makes "pack more productivity into a
smaller space" a real trade-off once density rises, and it is the natural home
for infrastructure to pay off into. The market-supply problem that prompted the
original idea was FIXED elsewhere — by the two-level firm budget (commit b4b5b3e),
which took every seed to its coverage target.

## Interaction with BL-512

BL-512's `per_province_firm_cap` bounds how many FIRMS anchor in a province; this
bounds how many BUILDINGS stand in it. They are different quantities and both are
provisional. Pin them together against the same sweep, or the two will be tuned
against each other by accident.


## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register) — drop the ceiling to where it bites, and let tech raise it

Ben, on the finding that capacity 103 stands more than four times above the 24 slots a province's
own geology could support: **"Drop it to where it bites"**, plus — *"Use technology for deeper
mines and denser facilities which use more of the cap."*

Two halves, and the second is the interesting one.

**The ceiling drops** to a value that actually constrains, measured against geology rather than
picked. NR-421 and NR-509 close with it.

**And technology becomes the thing that moves it.** *Deeper mines and denser facilities* is a tech
effect on how much of the cap a building consumes — which makes the province ceiling the first
**consumer** of a modifier subject that does not exist yet.

That is a direct answer to NR-524 (five modifier subjects wired to nothing): under Ben's ruling
each unwired subject must name the item that will wire it, and this item is the namer for a new
`facility_density` — or for `processing_yield`, if a denser facility is expressed as more output
per slot rather than fewer slots per building. **Which of the two is the design call owed here.**
BL-513.completion: COMPLETE 2026-08-21. Confirmed province-size-independent three times since (12.5535 after the 3x3 repartition, 12.5047 after organic borders, 12.2477 after absorption). BL-514.design:
## Held deliberately, awaiting Ben's look

Ben, 2026-08-21, on seeing province-grain rendering land:

> "I have a feeling that we should blend all tiles, not just within provinces,
> but hold off on that until I see what it looks like with larger provinces."

So this is **not** a decision deferred through inattention — it is a decision
Ben has explicitly sequenced behind evidence he does not have yet. Do not build
it, and do not fold it into a province-rendering task as a tidy-up.

## What it would mean

Today the blend stops at the province boundary by construction: vertices are
averaged within a province, and the seam between two provinces stays a seam
(softened to alpha 105, but present). Blending ALL tiles removes that stop —
the whole land surface becomes one continuous field, and province edges exist
only as the on-demand selection outline.

## Why the sequencing is right

The current seam is visible *because* provinces are small. At 3-5 tiles the eye
sees a dense clover mosaic, and the province edge is the dominant repeating
feature of the map. At **7-12 tiles** (the revised ruling, being built now) the
seams are far fewer and much longer, and the same alpha may read completely
differently — either as pleasing region definition, or as arbitrary lines
across continuous ground.

Which of those it is decides this item, and it cannot be decided from the
4-tile screenshots.

## What to have ready when Ben looks

- The same close-zoom framing as `province_blend_close.png`, at the new size.
- The map at play zoom, where the seam density is what actually reads.
- A capture with province edges at alpha 0 as the A/B — that is this item's
  proposal rendered, and it costs one constant to produce.

## The consequence to name if it goes ahead

Ocean and BUILT tiles are currently outside the blend by construction, which is
what keeps installations and coastline crisp. A global blend does not
automatically change that — but if the land reads as one field and buildings
still sit on visibly crisp hexes, the map still carries two visual languages
(NR-417). Worth deciding both together rather than in sequence.

## RULED — Ben, 2026-08-22 (UI session)

Ben, on being shown the province render at the 7-12 tile grain:

> "blur should cross province borders, it will probably look better"

and, asked whether the border line itself survives: **drop the stroke to 0**.
So this is the full form of the item, not the half — the land becomes one
continuous field and a province edge is drawn ONLY as the on-demand selection
outline. The alpha-105 stroke NR-417 called the one dial to move is now moved,
to zero.

This also settles NR-443: BL-514 and BL-520 were to be decided together rather
than in sequence, and they now have been. Texture is what carries terrain
legibility once the seam is gone.

The consequence the item named still stands and is NOT waived: ocean and BUILT
tiles remain outside the blend, so installations and coastline stay crisp. If
that reads as two visual languages once the land is continuous, that is the
next thing to look at, not a reason to delay this.

|---|---|
| Seeds | **Population centres**, which become the larger provinces |
| Boundaries | **Rivers, elevation difference, and sometimes roads** |
| Roads | A road **BINDS** — tiles a road links tend to share a province |
| Identity | **Derived from its lowest-id member tile** (Ben, 2026-08-21, revising the allocated-id answer) |
| Wilderness | **Hinterland provinces** — same boundary rules, no centre |
| When borders move | **Generation only**, fixed once the campaign starts |
| Elevation source | **Retain the generation heightmap** as a per-tile field (BL-517) |
| Size | **7-12 soft target**, boundaries win ties; **3-12 hard target** |
| Tiny provinces | **Do not reject them** — an island is allowed to be small |
| Water | Provinces are drawn over **ocean** too (BL-516) |

### Identity, revised 2026-08-21 — and why this is better than allocation

Ben first answered *an allocated id, created once and serialised*, then on reading the
determinism concern revised it to the **lowest-id member tile**. That is the stronger
choice, and it dissolves the problem rather than managing it:

- **Determinism comes free.** A derived id cannot be handed out in the wrong order,
  because it is not handed out at all. The NR-427 hazard — an allocator assigning ids
  in hash-map encounter order — stops being possible rather than being guarded against.
- **Nothing new is serialised.** No allocator state, no next-id counter, no save-format
  surface. `tile_province` is already rebuilt on read.
- **It is unique by construction**, since every tile belongs to exactly one province.

The cost it carries, and why that cost is now acceptable: a derived id CHANGES when the
province changes shape. That was the objection when borders looked like they might move
during the campaign. They do not — Ben ruled borders move during **generation only**. So
ids churn while the Era -1 sim redraws them (BL-518), and are **frozen before anything
outside generation can hold one**. A battle record, a march order or a save only ever
sees the settled id.

One consequence to carry into BL-518: when a province splits, each half derives a fresh
id from its own lowest tile, and the original id survives only on whichever half kept
that tile. That is a coherent answer to BL-518's open id question — reached on purpose
rather than discovered later.

### The constraint that still holds

The partition WALK must still be deterministic even though ids now derive from geometry.
`world::bodies` is an `unordered_map`, and iterating it unsorted once already fed
province ids in a container-dependent order — the leak was caught in
`build_province_partition` and fixed by sorting the body walk explicitly. Keep that.

### What this breaks that currently holds

`province.hpp` states, and `province_partition_harness` asserts, that a province
is "a contiguous run of LAND tiles" that "never spans water". Ocean provinces
overturn both. The harness rows must be rewritten with the ruling, not quietly
deleted — a land-only assertion that stops being true should become a
water-aware assertion, not disappear.

Also: `province_of` currently returns 0 for ocean, and 0 is a real province id.
That collision is already handled for land by the `no_province` sentinel
(0xFFFFFFFF, BL-511's seam work); ocean membership must use the same discipline.

### Growth shape, proposed

1. **Seed** at each population centre; seed strength scales with centre scale (1-5).
2. **Grow** by cost-weighted flood fill, where crossing an edge costs:
   - a **river edge** (`tile_component::river_edges`, already a per-side bitmask —
     the right shape for a border) — expensive;
   - an **elevation difference** (BL-517's retained height) — expensive in
     proportion to the gradient;
   - a **road link** — CHEAP, because a road binds;
   - flat, road-free, river-free ground — ordinary.
3. **Hinterland**: land unclaimed when the centre-seeded fronts stop becomes its
   own provinces under the same cost rules, seeded from the least-accessible tile
   so hinterlands are shaped by terrain rather than by leftovers.
4. **Size**: 7-12 is a soft target expressed as a growth budget, not a clamp.
   Boundaries win ties. Hard target 3-12, and tiny provinces are kept, not merged
   away.

### Deferred to its own item, not built here

Ben: *"We can also use generation to edit province borders as wars are won."*
That is the Era -1 history sim redrawing provinces on conquest, and it belongs
with the sim rather than with the partition pass. Filed as **BL-518**.

### Reference measurements to beat

The 3x3 block partition it replaces, over 6 seeds: 21,161 provinces, mean 9.11,
97.90% in the 7-12 band, 109 under-floor (all true islands, proven), 336 over.
The organic partition will not match that spread and is not meant to — but the
comparison is the honest way to report what changed.


## CEILING RULED 2026-08-21 (Ben), after the absorption pass broke the old one

> "Let's raise the ceiling. We prefer up to 12 tiles, but up to 20 is permitted in
> rare cases."

So the 12-tile bound stops being a clamp and becomes a PREFERENCE, with a hard cap
at 20. That resolves the tension the absorption pass exposed: absorbing a singleton
into its cheapest neighbour could push a full province to 13, and the choice was
between clamping (dishonest), preferring a roomier neighbour (contradicts the
cheapest-edge rule the growth model is expressed in) and raising the bound. Ben
raised the bound.

**The shipped behaviour already satisfies this, and that is worth checking before
any code is written.** Measured after absorption across 6 seeds: 22,401 provinces,
max 16, with 1,099 (4.9%) over 12. Max 16 is inside the new hard cap of 20, and
nothing currently produces a province larger than that. So the work is probably NOT
an algorithm change:

1. Say it. `province.hpp` calls 12 "the one size rule in this file that is a clamp"
   and `province_section_max_tiles` documents "a built province is 1-12 tiles" —
   both already conditionally false, and now deliberately so.
2. Assert it. A hard-cap assertion at 20 that FAILS if anything exceeds it, replacing
   the old absolute-12 row. The prefer-room variant behind `IO_ABSORB_PREFER_ROOM`
   can then be deleted, since the case for it was the ceiling breach.
3. Measure "rare". 4.9% over 12 is the current number; whether that counts as rare
   is Ben's, and it should be REPORTED by the harness rather than asserted against a
   threshold nobody has chosen.

## Ben's ruling (2026-08-21)

> "We can also draw provinces over the ocean, using 3-12 size coastal tile
> provinces. That creates another tile type, which is ok. We can have lakes,
> coasts, and oceans. Ocean provinces should be much larger, but not larger than
> say 80 tiles"

Two changes, and the first is the load-bearing one.

## 1. Water gains kinds: lake, coast, ocean

Today `terrain_composition::ocean` is a single value and every water tile is the
same thing. It becomes three, and Ben has accepted that explicitly ("that creates
another tile type, which is ok").

**This is an enum widening on a SERIALISED type**, so it follows the one-appender
rule: append, never renumber, or every existing tile record shifts meaning.

What reads `ocean` today and must be re-examined, one by one — this list is the
actual work of the item:

- `placement_rules::is_ocean_tile` and `can_place` (buildings refuse water).
- `non_extraction_stack_cap` (ocean is exempt).
- `road_generation.cpp`'s water-crossing rule. Sprint B2 landed
  `kMaxCrossingTiles`, which distinguishes a strait from open sea by counting a
  contiguous run — that distinction becomes expressible in the DATA rather than
  inferred from run length, which is strictly better.
- The blend (BL-511): ocean is currently outside it by construction, which is
  what keeps the coastline crisp against blended land.
- Every lens that colours water.
- `province.hpp`'s land-only invariant, which BL-515 overturns.

## 2. Provinces are drawn over water

- **Coastal** provinces: 3-12 tiles, the same band as land.
- **Ocean** provinces: much larger, capped at **80 tiles**.
- **Lakes**: Ben named them as a tile kind but did not rule what province a lake
  belongs to — its own, the surrounding land province, or a coastal one. That is
  the open question of this item.

## What has no answer yet, and does not need one to build this

Nothing can currently BE in an ocean province. Units are land-bound, buildings
refuse water, and BL-467's battle envelope assumes units standing in a province.
So on the day they land, ocean provinces are addressable empty space.

That is not an argument against them — a naval layer needs somewhere to happen,
and convoys already cross water (BL-458's interdiction is tile-pathed and could
extend to sea lanes). It IS an argument for building them without inventing a
naval model to justify them.

## Why this is a real item and not a rider on BL-515

It touches the tile enum, the placement rules, the road pass, the blend and every
water-colouring lens. BL-515 can be built against land-only provinces first and
extended to water once this lands; sequencing them apart keeps each reviewable.

BL-517.design:
## Ben's ruling (2026-08-21)

Elevation difference is one of the three boundary signals BL-515 grows provinces
against. Asked where it should come from — the existing categorical `landform`
(plains / highland / mountain / canyon / valley / crater / rift) or a retained
heightmap — Ben chose **retain the generation heightmap as a per-tile field**.

## Why the choice matters

`terrain_landform` is seven classes whose numeric order means nothing:
`mountain = 2` and `canyon = 3` are not one step apart in height. A boundary rule
keyed to it can only ask "are these two tiles the same class?", which draws
borders around terrain TYPE rather than terrain SHAPE — and a watershed is a
shape.

The heightmap already exists. Tile generation Pass 1 computes it, and
`GENERATION_LEDGER.md` exposes it through `generate_body_tiles`'s optional
`generation_record`. It is then thrown away.

## The tension worth naming

`GENERATION_LEDGER.md` states a deliberate data lifetime for those intermediates:
**regenerate on demand, do not persist**. Retaining height contradicts that
stance for one field.

The justification: height stops being a generation intermediate the moment a
downstream system reads it. BL-515 makes it an input to the partition, so it
becomes world state rather than a breadcrumb. That reasoning belongs IN
`GENERATION_LEDGER.md` as part of landing this — not left as an inconsistency for
a later reader to trip over and "fix" by deleting the field.

## Cost

A float per tile: 45,240 tiles on the homeworld, roughly 180 KB. Trivial in
memory. The real cost is the serialisation seam — one more per-tile field,
appended, with the round-trip proof the tile record already carries.

## Scope

- Retain height on `tile_component`, written by the pass that already computes it.
- Serialise it: appended, no existing field moved.
- Expose it to the Generation Ledger's field overlay, where it is already designed.
- Do NOT re-derive `landform` from it, and do NOT change any existing terrain
  rule. This item only stops throwing the number away.
BL-517.completion: COMPLETE 2026-08-21. Height captured from the pass that already computes it - bit-identical to generation_record::height, asserted rather than toleranced. sizeof(tile_component) 336 -> 340, exactly +4 with no padding waste, 176.7 KB across the 3x map. No RNG stream perturbed (composition, landform and deposits all byte-identical across two same-seed runs), and the spectator golden did not move. No serialisation was owed: there is no tile serialiser at all (NR-430). H5 stands guard that landform is NOT a function of height, so wiring height into the landform pass later would be reported.

BL-519.design:
## Ben's brief (2026-08-21)

> "Perhaps we should redesign tiles. This comes in two forms, we want to add basic
> texturing, and we want to allow for composite tiles. For example a mountain might
> have a forest or not."

Texturing is **BL-520**. This item is the composite half, and it is a data-model
change before it is anything else.

## The finding this item turns on

**A mountain with a forest is already expressible**: `composition = forest` ×
`landform = mountain`. What cannot be said is *"a ROCKY mountain that happens to be
forested"* — because the composition slot has been spent on the forest.

`terrain_composition` is doing three unrelated jobs at once:

| Job | Values today |
|---|---|
| **Substrate** — what the ground is made of | `barren`, `rocky`, `volcanic`, `metallic`, `regolith` |
| **Cover** — what is growing or lying on it | `forest`, `grassland`, `tundra`, `wetland` |
| **State** — what has happened to it | `urban`, `icy`, `ocean` |

`urban` is the proof, not the exception. It is documented as a **one-way transform**
that fires when a tile's building stack fills, and it OVERWRITES the composition —
so today, paving a metallic tile destroys the fact that it was metallic. That is a
slot conflict already shipped, and the split fixes it as a side effect: with an
orthogonal state, a city on metallic ground stays on metallic ground.

So this item does not add a concept. **It un-mixes one that got overloaded.**

## The proposed split — three axes, one of them unchanged

**1. `terrain_substrate`** — the geology. Fixed at generation, never transforms.
`barren`, `rocky`, `sedimentary` (new: the soil the cover axis needs to sit on),
`volcanic`, `metallic`, `regolith`, `icy` (as a substrate on airless bodies, not as
a cover).

**2. `terrain_landform`** — the shape. **Unchanged**: `plains`, `highland`,
`mountain`, `canyon`, `valley`, `crater`, `rift`. It already does exactly one job.

**3. `terrain_cover`** — what sits on the substrate, and CAN BE ABSENT. That
absence is the whole point: `none` is a first-class value, and "a mountain with no
forest" stops being a different composition from "a mountain with one".

Cover candidates, with the substrate each reads on:

| Cover | Reads on | Why it earns a slot |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | anything | Bare ground is a real answer, not a missing one |
| `grass` | sedimentary, barren | Thin cover on real ground; today a composition |
| `scrub` | barren, rocky, sedimentary | The half-step that makes a forest line gradual instead of a hard edge |
| `forest` | sedimentary, rocky, volcanic, tundra-ish | Ben's example. Sub-kinds (boreal / temperate / jungle) are a later axis, not a wider enum |
| `marsh` | sedimentary, on low landforms | `wetland` today; genuinely a cover, and it wants valley/plains |
| `snow` | anything | Falls out of latitude x BL-517's retained height with no new input |
| `dunes` | barren, rocky | Explains why some barren tiles are workable and others are not |
| `ash` | volcanic | A hazard reading rather than a resource one |
| `salt` | barren | Dry-basin cover; a home for a salt deposit if one is ever restored |

Deliberately NOT cover: `urban` (a state), `ocean` (a water kind — BL-516), and
`permafrost` (a sub-surface property that gates build cost, and wants its own flag
if it is ever wanted at all).

## The two shapes that are NOT area cover

Recorded here so the item is not later widened to swallow them:

- **Edge features** live BETWEEN tiles. `tile_component::river_edges` is already a
  per-side bitmask, and BL-515 draws province borders against it — the precedent
  exists and works. Cliffs / escarpments and coastline fit the same shape. These
  are what make a map read as terrain rather than as tiles.
- **Point features** occupy one tile and do not tile-fill: volcano cone, oasis,
  spring, cave mouth, waterfall. Cheap, disproportionately legible, and they are
  what a player names a place after.

Both are separate items when wanted. This one is the area axes only.

## Migration — and the reason it is cheaper than it looks

**There is no save format.** `read_procurement`, `read_history_log` and the order
book are the only flat-binary streams, and tiles are never written — they are
regenerated from the seed (confirmed while landing BL-517, NR-430). So there is no
save migration, no version bump, and no compatibility window. The whole cost is
in-code call sites.

Measured: **330 references to `composition` across 49 files**, concentrated in
`tile_generation.cpp` (60), `terrain_combat.cpp` (32), `placement_rules.cpp` (32),
`corporation_generation.cpp` (18), `nation_generation.cpp` (15), and the UI
(`hex_render` 14, `presentation` 13, `generation_ledger` 12).

**Staging strategy, and it is what makes this landable in one pass:** keep a
derived accessor

```cpp
terrain_composition tile_component::composition() const;   // substrate + cover -> the old value
```

so every existing call site keeps compiling and behaving while the axes land
underneath. Then migrate call sites by MEANING, in batches, and delete the accessor
last. A call site asking "is this forest?" usually means "is there timber here?"
(cover) or "can I build on it?" (substrate) — and which one it meant is exactly the
information the overloaded enum was losing.

## What moves, by system

- **Resources.** `RESOURCES.md` ties deposits to terrain affinity. Timber follows
  `cover = forest`; agricultural produce follows `cover = grass|marsh` on
  sedimentary; every ore follows the SUBSTRATE. This is the split paying for
  itself — a forested metallic mountain can now carry both timber and ore, which
  the single slot made impossible.
- **Lenses.** Colour by substrate, pattern by cover — which is also exactly what
  BL-520's texturing wants, so the two compose.
- **Placement.** `non_extraction_stack_cap` is per composition today; it becomes a
  substrate base with a cover modifier (forest is harder to build on than the rock
  beneath it).
- **Urban.** Becomes a state flag rather than a composition value, and STOPS
  destroying the geology underneath. BL-366's one-way-transform rule survives
  unchanged in meaning.
- **Generation.** A new cover pass, deterministic and seeded, running after
  landform and before deposits (deposits read both axes).

## Open questions for Ben

1. **Is cover binary or graded?** A density scalar (sparse -> dense forest) would
   let the texture and the timber yield share one number, but it is a second new
   field.
2. **Does `tundra` survive as a cover, or is it just `scrub`/`none` on frozen
   ground at high latitude?** It reads more like a climate outcome than a thing.
3. **Is `urban` a state axis or a cover value?** Filed above as a state, because a
   city has a substrate underneath it — but it is Ben's call.
4. **Should the derived `composition()` accessor be permanent or deleted?**
   Permanent is a smaller diff and a lasting lie; deleted is honest and a longer
   migration.

New harness tools/verify/tile_axes_harness.cpp (13 checks). THE STRUCTURE THAT MADE IT LANDABLE: Pass 4a (the band/moisture tables) is unchanged draw-for-draw and now returns an internal `biome`; Pass 4c decomposes it onto the axes with NO RNG stream (density is a stateless fold); Pass 4d - the only new behaviour - dresses ground the biome table left BARE, also with no stream. BL-520.design:
## Ben's brief (2026-08-21)

> "This comes in two forms, we want to add basic texturing, and we want to allow
> for composite tiles."

BL-519 is the composite half. This is the texturing half.

## Why this is easier AFTER the axis split, not harder

Texturing the current model means covering **12 compositions x 7 landforms = 84
combinations**, each hand-authored, most of them nonsense (`metallic` x `crater`
occurs on airless bodies only; `urban` x anything is a paved tile whose landform
stopped mattering the moment it transformed).

Texturing the split model means **one base texture per substrate** (7-ish) plus
**one overlay pattern per cover** (9-ish), composited at draw time. Sixteen
authored assets instead of eighty-four, and the combinations that were never drawn
still render correctly because they compose rather than being enumerated.

That is the argument for sequencing this behind BL-519. It CAN be built first,
keyed to the current composition — but it would be authored twice.

## Scope: BASIC texturing

Ben said basic, and the word is load-bearing given what already ships:

- The canvas draws flat-filled convex polys plus, since BL-511, a per-vertex
  Gouraud blend across a province's tile mixture. That blend is the reason texture
  needs care: **a texture and a colour blend fight each other**. The blend smooths
  across tiles; a texture asserts where one tile ends.
- The resolution: texture the SUBSTRATE (which the blend already averages) and
  pattern the COVER (which is per-tile and should read as per-tile). A forest edge
  is information; a rock-to-rock seam is not.

Out of scope, and named so it is not assumed: no normal maps, no lighting model,
no seasonal variation, no animated water. `TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md` scopes the
prototype to ImGui draw lists, and a texture atlas sampled through
`ImDrawList::AddImage` is the ceiling here.

## What it touches

`src/ui/hex_render.cpp` (14 composition references), `src/ui/presentation.cpp`
(13 — identity colours live there, not in `icons.hpp`), `src/ui/body_surface_canvas.cpp`
(the fill and blend pass), and `docs/ui/PLANETARY.md`.

The LOD path matters: BL-269's coarse LOD already drops the province edge stroke
at far zoom because a 1px stroke on a 7px hex is noise. A texture needs the same
treatment, and probably a lower threshold — a sampled pattern on a 7px hex is
worse than noise, it is moire.

## Open questions

1. **Does texture survive the map lenses, or do lenses replace it?** Eleven overlay
   modes recolour the map; a texture underneath a Country-lens fill either reads as
   depth or as dirt.
2. **Atlas or procedural?** An atlas needs art assets this project has none of.
   A procedural hatch/noise per cover needs none and suits the hand-drawn vector
   idiom `ICONS.md` already establishes.
3. **Does the province blend survive texturing at all**, or does texture replace
   the blend as the thing that makes the map read as terrain? That is a real fork
   and it interacts with BL-514 (blend all tiles), which is HELD pending Ben seeing
   the organic borders.
BL-520.resolution:
LANDED 2026-08-21, sequenced behind BL-519 exactly as the item argued: the split turned 84 hand-authored combinations into 13 composable marks. PROCEDURAL, not an atlas - the project has no art assets and a hashed field of marks suits the hand-drawn vector idiom.

The resolution the item specified is what shipped: GRAIN on the substrate (4 kinds - dot stipple, bedding strokes, fracture chips, and metallic in pale ink so it reads specular), PATTERN on the cover (9 kinds), 2-5 marks scaled by cover_density. Ocean draws nothing, deliberately - a mark on water would read as the animated water the item excludes. Mark placement is hashed from GRID coordinates, never screen position, or the ground crawls under a pan and two wrap copies of one tile disagree.

LENSES: texture SURVIVES all of them at 0.45 strength rather than being replaced (NR-456). The precedent is BL-231's landform relief one channel over. What stops it reading as dirt is not the 0.45 but the ink derivation - each mark's colour comes from the tile's OWN drawn fill pushed toward a per-cover target, so under Country a mark is that nation's colour darkened, shading on the block rather than a competing colour. The same derivation makes the fog wash and survey dim free.

LOD: off below draw_r 14px, ramping to full at 22px - STRICTER than BL-269's 7px, and deliberately: a small hex fill is merely invisible, a small sampled pattern is MOIRE. Verified arithmetically that it returns 0 at r=7, so the whole-grid view is pixel-identical to pre-BL-520.

NOT VERIFIED VISUALLY - the container cannot build the GUI, so nothing has been rendered (NR-457). scripts/verify/tile_texture.lua is added and named in the verifier-visual skill, CAPTURE-ONLY with no golden blessed, since blessing an unseen frame pins whatever got built. Still open and Ben's: does the province blend survive texturing at all, or does texture replace the blend as the thing that makes the map read as terrain (the item's open question 3, which also decides BL-514).

## The shape

Post SYNTHETIC POINTER INPUT INTO ImGui'S OWN EVENT QUEUE, in `app::render()` between
`ImGui_ImplSDL3_NewFrame` and `ImGui::NewFrame`. The point is that it drives the **real** input
path — the canvases' own hit-tests, the real click handlers, the real panel mouse capture — so a
passing script is evidence about the thing a player touches. A parallel test seam that calls the
handler directly would prove only that the handler works when called, which was never in doubt.

Lua surface: `verify.click`, `verify.double_click`, `verify.click_tile`, `verify.hover`,
`verify.tile_screen`, `verify.pointer_target`.

## Determinism is the hard part

ImGui promotes a press to a double-click by comparing `g.Time` against `MouseDoubleClickTime`.
Left alone, whether an injected pair reads as two singles or as one double would depend on FRAME
TIME — which is exactly the kind of non-determinism the project does not accept. `inject_pointer`
forces that window per press (0 never chains, FLT_MAX always does) and restores it afterwards.

Injection is a **no-op until a script uses it**, so interactive play and every pre-BL-521 script
stay byte-identical.

## What it deliberately does not do

Panels are still not clickable **by name** — that needs a target registry mapping a control's
identity to its screen rect, which is a separate item (NR-454). This closes the live-check class
for CANVASES only.

## Note on how it was built

Because the design field was already corrupt when the work started, the API shape is the
implementing agent's rather than an authority's — flagged as novel work at the time (NR-453).
